content:
In my previous article I talked about my very debut in the coding world and why Rust is my choice (I just love Rust).
The most important lesson Since I finished RareCode , for about a week I struggled a lot. I was wondering: “What’s next?”.
I’ve tried to:
read a book (Learn Rust in a Month of Lunches ) that I’ve already talked about, and it was really valuable until the chapter covered a topic that I haven’t previously understood and practiced. follow tutorials, but it was really short because I just don’t like that. start a personal project with Leptos , well… my skills need some improvements before Leptos. I didn’t understand a lot of things while going through the documentation. My attempt to create a personal project was maybe a little bit too rushed. But because of that I’ve found Codewars , did a lot of kata (all the 8 kyu in Rust) and progressed a lot.
So what’s the lesson here?
I can summarize it in one single word: PRACTICE.
You probably know the famous proverb: “Practice makes perfect”. In my experience, it’s more something like: “Practice makes progress”. If you chase perfection, you’ll be stuck even before the starting line.
Practice, that’s the most important word that’s related to progress, not just in code but everywhere.
Become an expert I’m not an expert. Absolutely not. Keep that in mind.
I’ve done some research with this single question in mind: “How can I improve my Rust skill without a limit?”, all I want is to keep learning Rust for a very long time, and always learn something new.
This is very close to the question: “How to learn?”.
In summary, all I want is to learn like an expert in learning. Something like that.
I’ve always loved learning new things. Like you I’m sure of that.
But because I’ve only one life (which could stop at any time btw) and only 24h/day, I think spending a little bit of time here and there to learn how great learners learn, and copy them is worth the time.
I’m talking about learning and how to become an expert because, first I want to improve in these areas, and second because this is the next part that comes right after PRACTICE.
Yes we have to practice to get better at what we are doing, but learning the meta skill of learning to be even better isn’t an option to reach the top.
“Work smart, not hard”. I don’t like this quote. Yes I want to work hard because I love it, because I have no other choice to achieve my dreams. You can work hard and smart. Why not!.
What’s next for me When I discovered Codewars , I’ve set myself the goal to complete all the kata in Rust (1185 right now). I already completed 148 (all the 8 kyu), and improved a lot with iterator and collections in Rust, but also in logic (which I was aiming for).
That goal isn’t going anywhere, but I’ll still modify it a little. Before I wanted to complete all the kata and then start some personal project.
After my research on learning, I now think that is not the better way for me to progress. The real goal isn’t to complete all the Codewars’s kata, it’s to create projects, build stuff. So, I’ll build some cool stuff and alongside complete the kata that are related to the problems/concepts that I want to learn. These problems and concepts will appear to me in my project.
The idea isn’t anymore learning by following a premade path, but learning because I need to, to solve my current problem in my project.
My project There is one thing that annoys me a little lot with Rust, and that is finding resources.
I’m learning Rust, and the more I learn Rust the more I love it. So I want to learn even more…
The Rust community is incredible, a lot of people create content inside/for the community, like crate, videos, books, articles, documentations, tools, etc.
Some “resources” are easy to find. If I tell you about Jon Gjengset , you know him, you just can’t miss him in the Rust ecosystem, same for The Book . Another example, even a beginner like me now knows some famous crate (even without the required level to use it) like tokio or serde .
But what if you have a very specific need?
I don’t want to create this project for me or for beginners but for the community. The expert in embedded devices that might need something very specific, the intermediate in Rust who wants to learn Web3, the beginner in code (hey that’s me) that probably needs to review the same thing 91422945495734957 times before it finally makes sense.
Rust is such an amazing language, the community is awesome, I love both of them. So I want to create something right now that can help you and me, find the resources that we are looking for.
I can’t build an amazing thing with just 1 month in the coding area. But by working hard, I can surely create something that works even if it’s not as beautiful as that website .
If you don’t have yet guessed what’s my project, it’s just a DB that stores Rust’s resources.
The idea at the beginning is that the community can add some resources (with a description, some tags, and the link will also be useful), and then the community can up vote or down vote the resource, submit improvement in the description and leave comments.
The idea is just to have a place to find something that you need without digging for hours and ending with nothing.
I will stream on Twitch and YouTube everything that I build.
And of course, it will take a long time before this solution really helps you. I can’t add all the resources alone, and also, as a beginner knowing if X resource is bad or not is impossible. That’s why it will take a long time. I need the more people possible to just add resources, vote for it to have better search results, to comment and suggest improvement for the description/how to use well the resource.
I have great ambitions with this project. It will take years but it’s worth to try.
The final idea and why The vision: Everyone can learn Rust for free, from my grandmother, to the tech team of a billion dollars company.
That means from the complete beginner in code, to a team that know how do the works in production. They can all learn something to be better.
The beginner in code is the starting line that show the whole idea. From beginner to a specialist in a chosen domain that get hire by a company, for free.
Why: I love to learn and to teach things. So at first I thought to create a business around teaching Rust (when I’ll have the level required).
But after, coding every day for hours, and love more and more Rust, I change my mind.
I’ll take JS in example because I know a little bit about that language. For JS there are tons of online courses and bootcamps. People do that because it print money (if really good). In some way I feel that do something bad to JS, I like online courses/I’m not against it, but it feel wrong to me to have that.
The thing is, it’s possible to learn JS for free. But online courses still exists because provide the experience that the teacher have.
For Rust we don’t have that (yet). Some things exists, but there aren’t many.
Think about that: what if, for free, everyone can learn from 0 Rust and become an expert that big company want to hire (like really want you). Provide something that’s so good for free that every online courses can’t even exist. And most important, if you don’t have much money, with hard work and enough time, you’ll change your life.
And here you should think, that’s a dream, and you’re right. That doesn’t mean that I’ll give up on that. It’s just one thing: the world is capitalist, so I’m going to need money to get by one way or another.
I’ll finish on that point. Think about what looks like the Rust ecosystem with that vision.
In my opinion, everyone will benefit from that (more programmer, more projects, more company that use Rust, better programmer…)

title: What I've learned after my first month of coding with Rust

content:
It took me around 8 months of procrastination, but at one point I finally finished 739 Rust exercises, as a non-programmer.
Let me tell you the story of a non-programmer (yet) learning Rust as his first language.
JavaScript, SaaS and illusions At the very beginning, I was wondering what to do in my life, what I really wanted to do in my life I mean. I watched on YouTube a video about AI and SaaS… I won’t go deep here, you can picture the story. Just some random beautiful thing that makes money, but the reality is different.
But, while AI was just a shiny object for me, SaaS on the other side was something that really interested me. So I started to learn JavaScript. And… it was terrible for me.
I don’t hate JS, or say that it’s a bad language, it’s just a really bad fit for me.
Maybe I learned JS for 3 months, with A LOT of procrastination. In 3 months I maybe really worked 15 days entirely.
By the time I procrastinated, I discovered Rust 🦀.
Rust, my love 💛 I don’t remember how I discovered Rust, but I remember that 5 minutes later, I was conquered.
I probably found a post or a video about it. And then, after understanding the core ideas of Rust, I was in love with it.
So from here I switched from JS to Rust… in my mind at least. Because my number one enemy in my life had returned again: PROCRASTINATION. It took me a long time to actually start to code.
Understand that, 0% of my procrastination was caused by Rust itself, it was just me.
At this point I was:
a non-programmer who loves Rust and procrastinates almost everything in his life If you only have the first two points, you’ll be fine with Rust.
The valley of death = PROCRASTINATION I procrastinated a lot at this moment, but I also was in love with Rust. So I dreamed about many things that I could build with it in the future. I created some roadmaps to learn and master Rust…
But sometimes I did something:
I started to work on the well-known “The Book ”, which is a really great book… but not for my level. After a few chapters, too many questions in my head were unanswered. To find some answers I started another book: “Learn Rust in a Month of Lunches ”, which is great, but like before, too many questions were still unanswered. I ended up learning about hardware, the big picture of how computers work. Since I discovered Rust maybe 5 months had already passed. And I didn’t code at all in Rust.
The first time coding in Rust The day I turned 24 I wanted to really change things, so I started RareCode .
As you can see there are two “parts” to my RareCode journey:
the first one I was still procrastinating the second one I stopped procrastinating and restarted from 0 all the exercises RareCode Like I said before I’m still not a programmer (I don’t make a living from my code, that’s my definition).
RareCode was for me something that I really needed. If you’re like me and don’t have yet the programmer mindset/way of thinking, this resource might be great for you.
The things I like about RareCode You practice a lot of times the same concepts. You re-use the previous concepts in more advanced exercises. When you learn how to code for the first time, just practicing a lot in different contexts the same concept is helpful to understand what you can or can’t do with this concept. And it’s just the beginning of course. The integrated AI. The AI in RareCode has in its context all the 739 exercises, your code and your errors. That means it can give you advice (not answers, also a great point) with in mind all the concepts you already covered. It just worked. With all the things I learned and even if I already forgot a lot, I’m confident enough to get my hands dirty and start a project on my own. Of course the code will be ugly, but between ugly code and nothing, the ugly code makes me progress. There’s no point “The things I didn’t like about RareCode”. It’s not perfect, and I’m a little sad that it’s not a solution from absolute beginner to more advanced Rust. But now I know that the normal Rust resources won’t be too advanced for me anymore. This is the first step, and a hard one. Some advice from a total beginner in Rust and not (yet) programmer These are the things that I think right now can be helpful to learn Rust whatever your level in programming:
Understand the hardware: I find it fascinating how hardware works, and even with very little knowledge about it I understand some Rust concepts better while I learn them. The compiler/borrow checker is not your enemy! It’s something that I never experienced, but I see a lot of people talking about the compiler like it’s evil or something. For me this is a really fun teacher that tells me everything I need to know. With a little help from AI, this is just incredible how many things I can learn from one single compiler message. Practice a lot and learn the Rust way. What I mean is, if you come from another language you have some paradigms about how coding works. And if you learn from scratch like me you’ll probably find a lot of resources that come from another language. I won’t say that it’s all bad but, like every language I do think there is a [Your Language Here] way, so in my case a Rust way to do things. Conclusion Is learning Rust as a first language harder than other languages?
I’ll say it depends. I tried a little bit of JS and for me it was total nonsense, nothing clicked in my head with JS. On the other side, everything clicked with Rust.
To answer that question I’ll say first, if Rust is a good fit for you it’s a good first point.
Then the only two things you need to learn Rust in my opinion are:
Loving Rust Being curious/don’t be afraid of deep dives, because there’s a lot to understand and learn. Avoiding hours of deep dive into how binary works for example, might not be a good move for the long term. All skills can be learned, Rust is just a (beautiful) way of applying the programming skill.
